## Introduction

This tutorial demonstrates a complete workflow for creating a spatial
sampling frame for Kolkata using `clusterComposer`.

The workflow consists of four stages:

1. Download the Kolkata boundary, building footprints and road network from
   Overture Maps.
2. Divide the area of interest into sections suitable for parallel processing.
3. Allocate population estimates to individual building footprints.
4. Run `clusterComposer` to generate the spatial sampling frame.

The code is provided as a worked example and is not run when the vignette is
built.

## 1. Download the Kolkata boundary, building footprints and roads data

This script downloads the Kolkata administrative boundary, building footprints
and road network from Overture Maps (Overture Maps Foundation, 2026). The data are saved locally as GeoPackage files for use in the subsequent stages.

```{r download-overture-data}

library(DBI)
library(duckdb)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(arrow)

con <- dbConnect(duckdb())
dbExecute(con, "INSTALL spatial;")
dbExecute(con, "LOAD spatial;")
dbExecute(con, "INSTALL httpfs;")
dbExecute(con, "LOAD httpfs;")
dbExecute(con, "SET s3_region='us-west-2';")

release <- "2026-10-21.0"

### Kolkata city boundary

division_path <- paste0("s3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/",release,"/theme=divisions/type=division_area/*")

city <- data.frame(admin_name = "Kolkata",search_name = "Kolkata",country = "IN")

dbWriteTable(con,"city_input",city,overwrite = TRUE)

division_sql <- sprintf("
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE admin_areas AS
SELECT
  c.admin_name,
  MIN(d.bbox.xmin) AS xmin,
  MIN(d.bbox.ymin) AS ymin,
  MAX(d.bbox.xmax) AS xmax,
  MAX(d.bbox.ymax) AS ymax,
  ST_Union_Agg(d.geometry) AS geometry
FROM read_parquet(
  '%s',
  filename = TRUE,
  hive_partitioning = 1
) d
JOIN city_input c
  ON d.country = c.country
 AND (
      d.names.primary = c.search_name
      OR d.names.common['en'] = c.search_name
 )
WHERE d.is_land = TRUE
GROUP BY c.admin_name;
", division_path)

dbExecute(con, division_sql)

# save the boundary as Parquet
dbExecute(con, "
COPY admin_areas
TO 'admin_unit_kolkata.parquet'
(FORMAT PARQUET);
")

# convert the boundary to sf object
admin <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "
  SELECT
    admin_name,
    ST_AsWKB(geometry) AS geometry
  FROM admin_areas
  "
)

admin$geometry <- st_as_sfc(admin$geometry,EWKB = TRUE,crs = 4326)
admin <- st_as_sf(admin)

# save Kolkata boundary as .gpkg
st_write(admin,"admin_unit_kolkata.gpkg",delete_dsn = TRUE)

### BUILDINGS

building_path <- paste0("s3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/",release,"/theme=buildings/type=building/*")

building_sql <- sprintf("
COPY (
  SELECT
    a.admin_name,
    b.id,
    b.names.primary AS primary_name,
    b.height,
    b.geometry
  FROM read_parquet(
    '%s',
    filename = TRUE,
    hive_partitioning = 1
  ) b
  JOIN admin_areas a
    ON b.bbox.xmax >= a.xmin
   AND b.bbox.xmin <= a.xmax
   AND b.bbox.ymax >= a.ymin
   AND b.bbox.ymin <= a.ymax
   AND ST_Intersects(b.geometry, a.geometry)
)
TO 'buildings_kolkata.parquet'
(FORMAT PARQUET);
", building_path)

dbExecute(con, building_sql)

### ROADS

transport_path <- paste0("s3://overturemaps-us-west-2/release/",release,"/theme=transportation/type=segment/*")

roads_sql <- sprintf("
COPY (
  SELECT
    a.admin_name,
    r.id,
    r.names.primary AS primary_name,
    r.class,
    r.subclass,
    r.geometry
  FROM read_parquet(
    '%s',
    filename = TRUE,
    hive_partitioning = 1
  ) r
  JOIN admin_areas a
    ON r.bbox.xmax >= a.xmin
   AND r.bbox.xmin <= a.xmax
   AND r.bbox.ymax >= a.ymin
   AND r.bbox.ymin <= a.ymax
   AND ST_Intersects(r.geometry, a.geometry)
)
TO 'roads_kolkata.parquet'
(FORMAT PARQUET);
", transport_path)

dbExecute(con, roads_sql)

# disconnect from DuckDB connection
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

### save buildings as gpkg

bld <- read_parquet("buildings_kolkata.parquet")
bld_geometry <- st_as_sfc(bld$geometry,crs = 4326)
bld_sf <- st_sf(bld[, setdiff(names(bld), "geometry")],geometry = bld_geometry)
st_write(bld_sf,"buildings_kolkata.gpkg",delete_dsn = TRUE)

### save roads as gpkg

roads <- read_parquet("roads_kolkata.parquet")
roads_geometry <- st_as_sfc(roads$geometry,crs = 4326)
roads_sf <- st_sf(roads[, setdiff(names(roads), "geometry")],geometry = roads_geometry)
st_write(roads_sf,"roads_kolkata.gpkg",delete_dsn = TRUE)
```

## 2. Divide the area of interest into sections

`clusterComposer` processes area-of-interest sections in parallel. This script
uses major roads and railways to divide Kolkata into sections. Large sections
are split further according to their building counts.

For efficient processing, approximately 1,000 buildings, or around 5,000
people, per section is recommended.

```{r create-aoi-sections}

library(arrow)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)

# read in roads data - this will be used to split the city unit into sections
roads_all <- st_read("roads_kolkata.gpkg")
roads_sf <- roads_all[roads_all$class %in% c("motorway", "trunk", "primary", "secondary", "tertiary","light_rail","monorail","tram"),"geom"]

# read in city boundary
admin <- st_read("admin_unit_kolkata.gpkg")

# create sections using major roads and rail
sections <- c(st_geometry(roads_sf),st_geometry(st_boundary(admin)))
lines <- st_union(sections) 
lines <- st_node(lines)
poly_strata <- st_polygonize(lines)
polygons <- st_collection_extract(poly_strata, "POLYGON")
polygons <- st_cast(polygons, "POLYGON")
polygons_sf <- st_as_sf(polygons)
polygons_sf <- polygons_sf[!st_is_empty(polygons_sf), ]
polygons_sf <- st_make_valid(polygons_sf)
#polygons_sf <- st_transform(polygons_sf, 4326) 
polygons_sf$area <- st_area(polygons_sf)
# merge small polys into neighbours
thresh <- 50000
repeat {
  small_idx <- which(as.numeric(polygons_sf$area) < thresh)
  if (length(small_idx) == 0) break
  merged_any <- FALSE
  for (i in small_idx) {
    nbr_idx <- st_intersects(polygons_sf[i, ], polygons_sf)[[1]]
    nbr_idx <- setdiff(nbr_idx, i)
    if (length(nbr_idx) == 0) next
    shared_len <- sapply(nbr_idx, function(j) {
      shared <- st_intersection(
        st_boundary(st_make_valid(st_geometry(polygons_sf[i, ]))),
        st_boundary(st_make_valid(st_geometry(polygons_sf[j, ])))
      )
      sum(as.numeric(st_length(shared)))
    })
    if (max(shared_len) == 0) next
    target <- nbr_idx[which.max(shared_len)]
    st_geometry(polygons_sf[target, ]) <- st_union(
      st_make_valid(st_geometry(polygons_sf[target, ])),
      st_make_valid(st_geometry(polygons_sf[i, ]))
    )
    polygons_sf <- polygons_sf[-i, ]
    merged_any <- TRUE
    break
  }
  if (!merged_any) break
}
polygons_sf <- polygons_sf[!st_is_empty(polygons_sf), ]
# check count of bfs in each section - reading from file much quicker than st_intersection
polygons_sf$bld_count <- NA
for(i in 1:nrow(polygons_sf)){
  polygons_sf$bld_count[i] <- nrow(sf::st_read(paste0("buildings_kolkata.gpkg"),
                                               wkt_filter = st_as_text(st_geometry(polygons_sf[i,]))))
}

# split sections with more than 1000 buildings 
# define number of splits per section from building count
polygons_sf$n_split <- case_when(
  polygons_sf$bld_count <= 1000  ~ 1L,
  polygons_sf$bld_count <= 2000 ~ 2L,
  polygons_sf$bld_count <= 3000 ~ 3L,
  polygons_sf$bld_count <= 4000 ~ 4L,
  polygons_sf$bld_count <= 8000 ~ 8L,
  polygons_sf$bld_count <= 16000 ~ 16L,
  TRUE                           ~ 32L
)
to_split <- polygons_sf[polygons_sf$n_split>1,]
split_polygons <- vector("list", nrow(to_split))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(to_split))) {
  poly <- to_split[i, ]
  n_split <- as.integer(poly$n_split[1])
  bb <- st_bbox(poly)
  width <- as.numeric(bb["xmax"] - bb["xmin"])
  height <- as.numeric(bb["ymax"] - bb["ymin"])
  aspect_ratio <- max(width, height) / min(width, height)
  if (aspect_ratio >= 2) {
    grid_n <- if (width >= height) c(n_split, 1L) else c(1L, n_split)
  } else {
    grid_n <- switch(
      as.character(n_split),
      "1"  = c(1L, 1L),
      "2"  = if (width >= height) c(2L, 1L) else c(1L, 2L),
      "3"  = if (width >= height) c(3L, 1L) else c(1L, 3L),
      "4"  = c(2L, 2L),
      "8"  = if (width >= height) c(4L, 2L) else c(2L, 4L),
      "16" = c(4L, 4L),
      "32" = if (width >= height) c(8L, 4L) else c(4L, 8L)
    )
  }
  grid <- st_sf(grid_id = seq_len(prod(grid_n)), geometry = st_make_grid(poly, n = grid_n, what = "polygons"))
  pieces_geom <- suppressWarnings(st_intersection(st_geometry(poly), st_geometry(grid)))
  pieces_geom <- pieces_geom[!st_is_empty(pieces_geom)]
  if (any(st_geometry_type(pieces_geom) == "GEOMETRYCOLLECTION")) pieces_geom <- suppressWarnings(st_collection_extract(pieces_geom, "POLYGON"))
  pieces_geom <- pieces_geom[st_geometry_type(pieces_geom) %in% c("POLYGON", "MULTIPOLYGON")]
  pieces_geom <- pieces_geom[!st_is_empty(pieces_geom)]
  original_attributes <- st_drop_geometry(poly)
  pieces <- st_sf(original_attributes[rep(1L, length(pieces_geom)), , drop = FALSE], grid_id = seq_along(pieces_geom), geometry = pieces_geom)
  original_area <- as.numeric(st_area(st_union(poly)))
  pieces <- st_make_valid(pieces)
  pieces_area <- as.numeric(st_area(st_union(pieces)))
  split_polygons[[i]] <- pieces
}
# create an sf object with both unsplit and split polygons
unchanged_polygons <- polygons_sf[polygons_sf$n_split == 1, ]
unchanged_polygons$grid_id <- NA_integer_
names(unchanged_polygons)[names(unchanged_polygons) == attr(unchanged_polygons, "sf_column")] <- "geometry"
attr(unchanged_polygons, "sf_column") <- "geometry" 
polygons_final <- dplyr::bind_rows(unchanged_polygons, split_polygons)
polygons_final <- st_cast(polygons_final, "MULTIPOLYGON")
polygons_final <- st_cast(polygons_final, "POLYGON", group_or_split = TRUE)
polygons_final$area <- st_area(polygons_final)
# merge any small polys created during splitting into neighbours
thresh <- 50000
repeat {
  small_idx <- which(as.numeric(polygons_final$area) < thresh)
  if (length(small_idx) == 0) break
  merged_any <- FALSE
  for (i in small_idx) {
    nbr_idx <- st_intersects(polygons_final[i, ], polygons_final)[[1]]
    nbr_idx <- setdiff(nbr_idx, i)
    if (length(nbr_idx) == 0) next
    shared_len <- sapply(nbr_idx, function(j) {
      shared <- st_intersection(
        st_boundary(st_make_valid(st_geometry(polygons_final[i, ]))),
        st_boundary(st_make_valid(st_geometry(polygons_final[j, ])))
      )
      sum(as.numeric(st_length(shared)))
    })
    if (max(shared_len) == 0) next
    target <- nbr_idx[which.max(shared_len)]
    st_geometry(polygons_final[target, ]) <- st_union(
      st_make_valid(st_geometry(polygons_final[target, ])),
      st_make_valid(st_geometry(polygons_final[i, ]))
    )
    polygons_final <- polygons_final[-i, ]
    merged_any <- TRUE
    break
  }
  if (!merged_any) break
}
polygons_final <- polygons_final[!st_is_empty(polygons_final), ]
polygons_final$section_id <- seq_len(nrow(polygons_final))
polygons_final <- polygons_final |>
  dplyr::select(-n_split, -grid_id)
# recalc bf count
polygons_final$bld_count <- NA
for(i in 1:nrow(polygons_final)){
  polygons_final$bld_count[i] <- nrow(sf::st_read(paste0("buildings_kolkata.gpkg"),
                 wkt_filter = st_as_text(st_geometry(polygons_final[i,]))))
}

# save sections
st_write(polygons_final,"kolkata_sections.gpkg")
```

## 3. Allocate population to building footprints

This script disaggregates population from a 100-metre population raster (Bondarenko et al., 2026) across the building footprints whose centroids fall within each raster cell.

In this example, population is allocated in proportion to building footprint
area. Alternative population-disaggregation methods could be used.

The population raster data can be downloaded from here and saved in a folder called `pop` inside your project/working directory: https://hub.worldpop.org/geodata/summary?id=73809 

```{r prepare-building-population}

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(arrow)
library(terra)

# read in Kolkata buildings
bf <- st_read("buildings_kolkata.gpkg")

# occasionally there are multipolygon buildings, e.g. a company's complex
# so cast all buildings to polygons, this will split up multipolygons with one row per individual polygon
n_parts <- lengths(st_geometry(bf))
mp <- n_parts > 1
bf <- rbind(st_cast(bf[!mp, ], "POLYGON", warn = FALSE),st_cast(bf[mp, ],  "POLYGON", warn = FALSE))

# create building centroids to identify each buildings' grid cell in the pop raster
bf_cent <- sf::st_centroid(bf)
bf_cent$cell_id <- NA
bf_cent$pop_cell <- NA
# read in pop raster
pop <- terra::rast("pop/ind_pop_2027_CN_100m_R2025A_v1.tif")
# extract raster cell ID and population value for each building centroid
ext <- terra::extract(pop,vect(bf_cent),cells = TRUE)
# attach cell ID and population to buildings
idx <- !is.na(ext[[2]])
bf_cent$cell_id[idx] <- ext$cell[idx]
bf_cent$pop_cell[idx] <- ext[[2]][idx]
# transfer this info from centroids object to footprints object
bf$cell_id <- bf_cent$cell_id
bf$pop_cell <- bf_cent$pop_cell
# calculate building area
bf$building_area <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(bf))
# calculate total building area per raster cell based on buildings whose centroids fall into a cell
cell_areas <- bf |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(cell_id)) |>
  group_by(cell_id) |>
  summarise(cell_bld_area = sum(building_area, na.rm = TRUE))
# join total building areas per cell to buildings object
bf <- bf |>
  left_join(cell_areas, by = "cell_id")
# disaggregate population equally across buildings within each cell based on building area
bf$pop_building <- bf$pop_cell * (bf$building_area / bf$cell_bld_area)
# set buildings outside populated cells to zero
bf$pop_building[is.na(bf$pop_building)] <- 0
# alternative to line above, drop buildings outside pop data cells (but then structure is not considered in cluster boundary delin)
#bf <- bf[!is.na(bf$pop_building),]
rm(ext,cell_areas,bf_cent,idx)

# save
st_write(bf,"buildingsWithPop_kolkata.gpkg")
```

## 4. Run `clusterComposer`

The prepared area-of-interest sections and populated building footprints are
then supplied to `clusterComposer`.

The example uses all but one of the available processor cores. Intermediate
files are retained so that completed sections can be reviewed if
an error occurs.

```{r run-cluster-composer}

library(sf)
library(clusterComposer)

# read in Area of Interest (aoi)
AOI <- sf::st_read("cities_data/kolkata_sections.gpkg")
# define number of computing cores
ncores <- parallel::detectCores() - 1

# run clusterComposer function
clusterComposer(aoi=AOI,
                bf_file_path = "cities_data/buildingsWithPop_kolkata.gpkg",
                run_id = "kolkata_20261117",
                output_file_path = "cities_output",
                n_cores = ncores,
                delete_temp_files = FALSE
)

```

## 5. Read in output geopackage to inspect the results

```{r evaluate-results-hist}

# read in output file produced by clusterComposer
sframe <- st_read("cities_output/kolkata_20261117_clusters.gpkg")

# histogram of population per cluster
hist(sframe$pop,breaks=100,xlab="population per cluster",main = paste("Number of clusters:", nrow(sframe)))

```

```{r population-figure, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="Distribution of population per cluster for the example Kolkata sampling frame."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/hist_population_per_cluster.png")
```


There are a total of 15,023 clusters in this example sampling frame for Kolkata.

The majority of clusters have a population size in the range of our target but there are some that are very large. Inspection of these clusters overlaid with building footprints (in QGIS) suggests that these unusually large clusters often contain large building footprints with high assigned population. For example, Sealdah Railway Station accounts for most of the population in the highest population cluster. ese results demonstrate that the method used to allocate population to building footprints can strongly influence the clusters generated by `clusterComposer`. Where suitable data are available, non-residential buildings should be identified during input preparation and assigned zero or appropriately low population values.

```{r evaluate-results-large-clusters}

length(sframe$pop[sframe$pop>350])

```
Of the 15,023 clusters, 65 have a population large than the maximum population per cluster of 350 people. 

```{r evaluate-results-hist-zoomed}

# histogram of population per cluster
hist(sframe$pop,breaks=200,xlab="population per cluster",main="",xlim=c(0,500))
abline(v = c(150, 350), col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(v = 250, col = "blue", lwd = 2)

length(sframe$pop[sframe$pop>=150&sframe$pop<=350])
length(sframe$pop[sframe$pop<150])


```


```{r population-zoomed-figure, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="Distribution of population per cluster for the example Kolkata sampling frame, truncated to 500 people. The blue line shows the target population per cluster, and the red lines show the minimum and maximum populations per cluster."}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/hist_population_per_cluster_zoomed.png")
```

93.6% of the total clusters (14,067 of 15,023) have population within the desired range. There are 891 clusters with population lower than the desired minimum. Many of these cover unpopulated areas such as the Pat Williamson Ground and large areas that mostly contain river. These low population clusters may also occur where combining with any neighbouring clusters would result in a cluster exceeding the maximum population per cluster. In this situation, the algorithm leaves the low-population cluster unchanged.
